title: This Is What Happens When 1,000 People Bury Their Underwear for Science - Nautilus
gist: A University of Zurich citizen-science project measured soil health across Switzerland by having more than 1,000 volunteers bury cotton underwear and teabags and track how much decomposed.

insights.claim: Healthy soil is a living ecosystem of bacteria, fungi, earthworms, and other organisms that recycle organic matter, aerate soil, and produce nutrients that plants need to grow.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Underlines that soil biological activity is a measurable input to agricultural productivity.

insights.claim: The rate at which buried cotton underwear decomposes serves as a proxy for how biologically active and healthy a patch of soil is.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A cheap, scalable indicator method that could be applied to monitor farmland soil quality.

insights.claim: University of Zurich ecologists enlisted more than 1,000 citizen scientists—half of them farmers—to measure soil health across Switzerland by burying underwear and teabags for 30 or 60 days.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a large-scale, low-cost model for distributed environmental monitoring.
insights.locator: Ecologists from the University of Zurich enlisted more than 1,000 citizen scientists
